title: SlotDrop: Group Reflection
subtitle: ITMGT 45.03, Group 1 | 27 November 2026
pages: SlotDrop began with a simple problem: a workshop can still have an empty seat even when the class is already going ahead, and that seat has no value once the session starts. In GC2, we built the journey that lets a customer discover a released seat, choose a quantity, accept a server quote and receive a saved booking. Our 105/100 result showed that the basic system and business case were working. For the Final, we chose to improve what happens between choosing seats and confirming them. A customer should have a short opportunity to finish their booking while the system gives the studio an honest count of what is still available.

Our USP is a server-enforced, ten-minute reservation of workshop seats that can expire and return those seats to availability. It is specific to a session with a fixed capacity and booking cutoff. A spreadsheet could record that someone wants two places, but it would not reliably coordinate simultaneous customers, enforce the same deadline across their browsers and preserve a consistent result when a request is retried. The intended on-screen proof is concrete: a reservation status and countdown in Selection or Checkout, fewer seats available to another customer, and a saved receipt after successful confirmation. An expired reservation should instead show a reason and allow the customer to choose again.

We have deployed the part that creates, reads and releases a persisted hold. It uses the server clock and the earlier of ten minutes or the studio's booking cutoff. A four-seat session with a two-seat hold therefore has two seats available to other customers. Once that hold expires, the server can return four seats without waiting for the customer's browser to run a timer. At this revision, the visible countdown and hold-to-booking conversion remain integration work. We are keeping that distinction explicit: working API responses establish the reservation rule, but we will only claim the complete USP when the customer can see it act and finish the same booking journey.

The one GC2 comment we selected was the reported first-visit delay of about 22 seconds. We prioritized it because the instructor will open the application independently, and a visitor waiting on a blank or loading screen cannot judge the work behind it. It also affects the first click of the live demo, which now carries 35% of the grade. GC2 had already praised our price checks, saved receipts, collaboration and financial analysis. Rewriting those working parts would have added risk while leaving the observed first-visit problem in place. Reliable access was the highest-impact improvement we could make to the experience that was actually evaluated.

We addressed that comment with a health route, a health-ping workflow configured every ten minutes, a pre-presentation warm-up and a local fallback. We have now observed successful scheduled runs, including an actual HTTP 200 response. A configured schedule and an observed request are different kinds of evidence, so we still need to check recent execution and first-load responsiveness before choosing the deployed site as our starting point. The laptop version uses the same application rules and persists its data between runs. Our plan is to choose a tested starting point before the defense, open the application and Owner screen in advance, and keep the alternative ready.

One difficult bug involved the relationship between a hold and an Owner edit. If the studio moved its booking cutoff earlier, an existing hold could retain its original, later expiry. That left two parts of the system making different promises about the same seat. We changed the cutoff edit so affected holds are shortened in the same transaction. Moving the deadline later does not restart a customer's reservation window. This taught us to check how an edit affects records that already exist, rather than verifying only that the new value appears correctly on the screen.

We also found a presentation problem when Home began reusing grouped workshop cards. The date-option styles had been scoped to Browse, so dates, prices and cutoffs ran together on Home. We added scoped Home styles and checked the cards at phone and desktop widths. It was a small change in code, but it showed how reuse can carry a hidden dependency. A shared renderer did not automatically bring the surrounding layout with it. We now check the actual screen after integrating a component, including its links, empty state and recovery behavior, instead of assuming that a passing API response guarantees a usable page.

The V2 tinker test exposed a problem with browser history: after a successful booking, Back could restore Checkout still saying "Saving" with both actions disabled. We changed the successful navigation to replace the completed form with the saved receipt, so Back returns to Selection. Invalid quantities also left session details saying "Loading" after validation had already stopped the request. They now identify Quantity, retain the loaded session and keep Continue disabled. These were useful reminders that a correct database result can coexist with a confusing screen. We checked the actual pages and saved-record count, rather than treating a lack of JavaScript errors as enough.

Our existing duplicate protection gave us a strong foundation for that work. Checkout saves a stable request identity before sending a booking, and the server returns the original receipt for an identical retry. The stored price and fee snapshots keep a later offer edit from rewriting an earlier receipt. We learned to separate a failed request from an uncertain result: if the server may already have saved the booking, sending a new request identity would create a different problem. The right recovery is to establish what happened to the original attempt. The same discipline must carry into consuming a hold, so converting a reservation cannot sell or reserve its seats twice.

Collaboration became most concrete at the handoff between Selection, Checkout and the booking service. Fran's hold endpoints alone cannot complete the customer journey; Janelle's quote and save functions must recognize the reservation, and Kat and Kaitlyn must carry the same session, quantity, hold ID and expiry across their screens. A boundary check still returned an unsupported holdId response, which exposed that gap clearly. We are using that result as an integration condition rather than hiding it behind a successful unit test. Kirsten's work on shared states and Chonel's Home handoff also need to be checked against the same server availability rule.

Our outside-group iPhone test on November 16 had already shown someone moving through the booking journey and saving a one-seat Bumi & Ashe booking for PHP 2,880. A separate readback matched that receipt in Owner. That gave us useful evidence that the GC2 flow could be followed outside our own development setup. It is still a snapshot of an earlier build, so we are retaining it while checking the changed paths directly. We learned to make each test answer a specific question: which record was saved, which seats changed, what the customer sees after returning, and how they can recover if their next action is refused.

The next business step would be a small pilot with one consenting studio. We would ask for actual released capacity, attendance, preparation cutoffs and costs, then reconcile SlotDrop bookings with the studio's direct sales. Our sourced studio references and simulated sessions do not establish a partnership or prove demand. We need to learn whether a discounted booking fills a seat that would otherwise stay empty, or simply moves a customer away from the studio's full-price channel. That question would determine whether we should extend the offer, change it or stop it before adding more suppliers and operational complexity.

This distinction changed how we read our money model. At the demo prices, two standard seats pay the studio PHP 4,860 after commission, while two buddy seats pay PHP 4,617. If both customers would have booked anyway, the studio gives up PHP 243. The lower price is useful only when enough bookings add attendance or improve the studio's overall contribution. We have not measured that incremental share, so the buddy rate remains a pilot assumption. We know more now about the difference between calculating a discount correctly and showing that the discount is a sound business decision.

In our four-week scenario, selling 32 of 64 released seats produces 28 bookings and PHP 8,532 in platform fees. After an assumed PHP 1,400 in booking support and PHP 6,000 in outreach and operations, SlotDrop keeps PHP 1,132 before founder time, taxes, future payment costs and refunds. At that same sales mix, break-even is about 27 seats; the downside can still lose money. Those figures are modeled outcomes, not sales we have achieved. Our decision is to retain the 10% commission for a one-studio pilot, use 27 of 64 released seats as the modeled break-even checkpoint, and expand only when actual costs leave both SlotDrop and the studio with a positive contribution.
